title: The Antikythera Mechanism
hook: In 1901, sponge divers uncovered a bronze relic from a shipwreck off Greece, but its purpose baffled scholars.

beats.label: THE CASE
beats.line: In 1901, sponge divers recovered a bronze gear-filled device from a shipwreck near Antikythera.

beats.label: CLUE 1
beats.line: The corroded fragments included 30 bronze gears, suggesting a complex clockwork.

beats.label: CLUE 2
beats.line: Analysis dated the device to around 100 BC, making it the oldest known analog computer.

beats.label: CLUE 3
beats.line: Its front dial displayed a 19-year Metonic cycle, aligning lunar months with the solar year.

beats.label: THEORY
beats.line: One theory proposes the mechanism predicted eclipses and planetary positions for navigation.

beats.label: THE TWIST
beats.line: Recent 3-D scans revealed hidden inscriptions pointing to a possible link with ancient Greek astronomer Hipparchus.

end.line: What could this ancient computer really have calculated for its makers?

description: A brief look at the mysterious Antikythera Mechanism and its secrets.

facts.claim: The Antikythera Mechanism was recovered in 1901 by sponge divers off Antikythera Island.
The device contains roughly 30 bronze gears forming a complex clockwork.
Radiocarbon dating places the mechanism around 100 BC.
One of its dials tracks the 19-year Metonic cycle aligning lunar and solar calendars.
High-resolution 3-D imaging has uncovered hidden inscriptions linking it to Hipparchus.
Scholars suggest it could predict eclipses and planetary positions for navigation.
